title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 Motorways with No Speed Limits and Car-Free Town Centres
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Using Germany's context-dependent approach to cars -- unrestricted motorways and car-banned medieval town centres -- as a guiding metaphor, Daisy Christodoulou argues that the debate about educational technology should not be pro- or anti-tech but context-sensitive. She updates her 2020 Teachers vs Tech argument: the primary justification for ed tech is scale -- technology is a great equaliser because quality variations within schools (and across classrooms) exceed quality variations between them, a problem money and smaller class sizes have not solved. But the Covid natural experiment revealed something equally important: even inconsistent in-person schooling outperformed remote screen-based learning, strongly suggesting that learning is social and embodied in ways that screens cannot replicate. For very young children especially, learning depends on eye contact, shared attention, imitation, and interactive back-and-forth -- conditions that screens struggle to approximate. Christodoulou's conclusion: use technology to achieve scale on tasks where consistency and delivery efficiency are paramount, but protect the human, social, and physical dimensions of learning that remain irreplaceable.
points: * The fundamental justification for education technology is scale: OECD data shows quality variations within schools exceed variations between schools -- technology can deliver consistent quality in ways that hiring more teachers or reducing class sizes cannot. * The Covid natural experiment was decisive: unlike remote working, telemedicine, and e-commerce (all of which accelerated permanently), remote learning did not displace in-person school -- parents rushed to return children and learning data confirmed they were right to. * Learning is social and embodied -- for young children, it depends on eye contact, shared attention, imitation, emotional connection, and interactive back-and-forth conversation -- conditions screens approximate poorly. * The pro-tech argument for fully personalised screen-based education fails on empirical grounds: no one has found a way to successfully educate students at scale with a human-light, tech-heavy alternative involving screens most of the time. * Context determines whether technology helps or hurts: use it where consistency and scale are the problem (the motorway); protect physical, social, human-led environments where embodied learning is essential (the town centre).
quotes: Is Germany a pro-car or an anti-car society? Obviously, the context matters. In some contexts, cars are the solution to a problem. In other cases, cars are the problem.
Technology can be a great equaliser. In its ability to deliver consistent quality at scale, it is perhaps the most democratic force in existence.
Even the inconsistent in-person school is still better than learning remotely on screen.
For very young children, there is a lot of evidence that learning relies on eye contact, shared attention, imitation, emotional connection, and interactive back-and-forth conversation.
We have to find ways of using technology to get scale, but for the majority of school education I don't think that will involve kids sitting at screens.
